cells.tense: Right now the weighing is here and the world can wait for it.
cells.ask: Set a timer for fifteen minutes, write what you already see, and end the page without a plan.
cells.core:
There's something you see before you say it, and holding it back is not a delay. When you sit with both sides first, you catch the thing that would have been wrong before it leaves your mouth. That pause is the work, not the slowing of the work. Decisions land well around you when you're the one who actually held them open first. Staying open like that usually costs something. Right now it's costing and it's working.

Nothing here is decided yet, and that sits fine with you. That part can go sideways other weeks. You can keep one small window open today. Not for good — just long enough to not rush the next thing. If you sit down to write and nothing wants closing when the timer goes, leave it open a while longer. That's not a quota you owe anyone.

cells.tense: In a few weeks this will be settled and it will have gone the way it should.
cells.ask: Give one open question a yes or a no for thirty days, and let a person you trust hold you to it.
cells.core:
You're holding what you see and it won't come out. Two versions go back and forth and you keep running the move after this one before you've made this one. All that holding was supposed to keep you ready. It's turned into rehearsing a room you're not in yet. The weighing isn't weighing anymore — it's bracing.

Nothing here is decided, and that no longer fits. Some of what you're carrying belongs to a decision that hasn't happened. Try one small yes or no today, and leave it alone afterward. If you pick one, you can still change it later. What you stop doing is running it again tonight.

cells.tense: You were in the middle of deciding this once, and you're still standing as if you hadn't moved.
cells.ask: Say one thing you're sure of to a friend, roughly, and let what they say back land.
cells.core:
What you see is right there and the room for saying it isn't. Something you were about to decide is still sitting in the draft pile. The thought hasn't gone anywhere. You just stopped using it.

It's not that the answer left. It's that saying it hasn't come back into reach yet, and pushing won't bring it. So don't grind at it. Do the thing that fills the tank — sleep, a walk, something you actually enjoy. When the energy comes back, it comes back here first. Before that, say one thing you're sure of out loud, even to yourself. The rest can wait for you.

cells.tense: You've been making the call as you go and calling it not having decided yet.
cells.ask: Pick one moment from the last week where you cast the deciding vote, and write down whose call it was.
cells.core:
You've been letting people around you work out what they think, one sentence at a time. When someone reaches a conclusion in front of you and calls it their own, that conclusion had a shape already, and you were the one holding it. You're not tracking this as yours. It runs anyway.

You haven't been keeping score. That's exactly why this one needs you in it. This isn't a problem to fix before you do anything. One small piece of it, over and settled. Next time someone reaches a conclusion near you and calls it theirs, look at the shape for a second. You'll know what to do from there.

A reader could reasonably say 'sometimes I just don't know yet and that's fine,' which is true and does not break the cells, because the seat condition is the same and I never say what happened at the replaced door or put a motive under it. The asks survive being wrong: each one is a plain act that can be done and cannot fail, and none makes anything conditional on the read landing. The sentence that served me more than them was any line about what a buried door cost or taught; I cut all of them.
